newsitem.title: ITALY: Armani's easy elegance takes fuss out of fashion.
newsitem.headline: Armani's easy elegance takes fuss out of fashion.

text.p: Italian designer Giorgio Armani took the fuss out of fashion in an elegantly easy-going menswear collection on Thursday, paring collars to the minimum and rolling jackets and shirts into one.
Armani's spring/summer 1998 ready-to-wear designs concealed buttons under the jacket breast and hid flapless pockets in vertical seams on neat, easy-fitting jackets.
Broad, straight-legged pants, often without pleats but with a clean crease, gave the collection a comfortable but elegant air, with linen, silks and taffeta for day and evening dress.

The silver-haired designer made use of the new shirt-jacket style which has made its way into mens' trends at the Milan shows, with jackets in light fabrics or shirts in heavier materials created to replace both garments.
Shirts had tiny mandarin collars and were often cut straight down the waist and worn outside trousers.
Colours were subtle navies, greys and creams, with misty greens and rich bronze also featuring in a collection which exuded an air of health and wholesomeness.

Beachwear included male sarongs worn with long, loose-fitting shirts and sandals, while the Armani Jeans collection was a bright two-tone line-up of rich red shirts and jackets over navy pants or shorts and vice versa.

The Armani event winds up the five days of shows which earlier in the week saw French designer Jean Paul Gaultier displaying in the Italian fashion capital for the first time with a flamboyant and dandified collection.

American Tom Ford -- by now a Milan veteran after several seasons heading up design at Gucci -- brought a sense of subtle luxury to the catwalk, reviving braces with a thin crocodile skin finish which joined in a single thong down the spine.
Black and white predominated at the Gucci show with dark, broad-shouldered suits cutting a tall, angular figure tailored at the waist and relieved by a pristine white shirt.
The cool alternative was a creamy white version over an ice white shirt, while gleaming tie pins added a subtle glimpse of opulence as they held square-tipped black ties in place.
Pants were mostly slimfit under single-vented suit jackets wide from the hip and tapered slightly to the shoe.
Ford's palette then moved round to hallmark Gucci bronze, smokey blue and silky shirts in red shot with green and black.
Risque underwear came in transparent brown, black and green with a modesty panel at the front of tight-fitting trunks.

Beachwear was less transparent but just as snug. Ice-white trunks cropped to the top of the thigh and pencil-strap pants were slashed at the hip or over the base of the spine and adorned with a sequinned buckle or the GG Gucci motif.
Early in the week Gianfranco Ferre unveiled an array of Mediterranean hues like earth tones and early-morning blues.

Ferre said he aimed for structure combined with a sense of physical freedom so lightweight jackets had moderate shoulder pads but then fell softly to the hip, while wide-legged trousers avoided being overtly baggy.

Miuccia Prada weighed in with more austere approach. Shirts buttoned to the collar and fell straight to stop below the hip. Pants stopped short of the ankle where they met heavy grey socks and shoes fastened with velcro.
Designers Domenico Dolce and Stefano Gabbana showed no such severity with a charming crumpled look for suits and jerseys.

Slim but unrestrictive jackets worn over wide pants gave a tailored but comfortable effect while innovations included the "one-and-a-half" breasted suit fastened deeper into the front panel than a single breasted jacket but not as far as a double.
